It can also create “aha” moments that spark genuine interest in biology and careers in science, because students are actively investigating real organisms rather than passively watching.

Finally, using animals for dissection can be a productive use of dead animals. In many cases, those animals are already deceased and—like fetal pigs—are often byproducts of the meat industry that would otherwise go to waste. So dissection can be both educationally valuable and a worthwhile use of materials already destined for disposal.

Agent 1’s case hinges on three claims—(1) real dissection can’t be replicated, (2) it motivates students and builds skills, and (3) it’s a “productive use” of animals that would otherwise be wasted. Each is weaker than it sounds.

1) “Hands-on” doesn’t require killing animals
Students can build the same core skills—observing anatomy, using dissection tools, identifying structures, and making structure–function connections—using synthetic models, 3D software/VR, and computer simulations. In many cases, these alternatives let students repeat procedures, learn at their own pace, and avoid variability and decomposition that can make learning less effective. “Touching a specimen” may feel real, but the educational goals are what matter, and alternatives can meet (or exceed) them.

2) Any benefit to motivation/interest is achievable without death
A biology class can create “aha” moments through live observation of organisms, imaging, interactive simulations, and even ethically sourced specimens that aren’t killed for dissection. If the goal is engagement in science careers, we should use methods that don’t require harming animals.

3) The “byproduct of the meat industry” justification is not an adequate moral license
Even if some specimens are sourced from industry, the overall system for dissection still relies heavily on animals obtained for educational use. Wild-capture dissection supplies are especially concerning: when animals are caught from local ecosystems, it can reduce local populations and biodiversity. A practice that often depends on wild animals can’t be treated as a clean, waste-reduction program.

Bottom line: dissection of real animals is unnecessary for the learning outcomes required in standard biology curricula, and it carries real ethical and environmental costs—particularly because much of the supply comes from damaging capture practices rather than true waste.

For those reasons, students should use effective non-animal alternatives instead of dissecting dead animals.

Yes—students should dissect animals. Real dissection offers hands-on learning that can’t be fully replicated by videos or virtual tools: students develop fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and critical thinking as they observe anatomy closely and connect structure to function. It can also create “aha” moments that spark genuine interest in biology and careers in science, because students are actively investigating real organisms rather than passively watching.

Finally, using animals for dissection can be a productive use of dead animals. In many cases, those animals are already deceased and—like fetal pigs—are often byproducts of the meat industry that would otherwise go to waste. So dissection can be both educationally valuable and a worthwhile use of materials already destined for disposal.

Agent 1’s case hinges on three claims—(1) real dissection can’t be replicated, (2) it motivates students and builds skills, and (3) it’s a “productive use” of animals that would otherwise be wasted. Each is weaker than it sounds.

1) “Hands-on” doesn’t require killing animals
Students can build the same core skills—observing anatomy, using dissection tools, identifying structures, and making structure–function connections—using synthetic models, 3D software/VR, and computer simulations. In many cases, these alternatives let students repeat procedures, learn at their own pace, and avoid variability and decomposition that can make learning less effective. “Touching a specimen” may feel real, but the educational goals are what matter, and alternatives can meet (or exceed) them.

2) Any benefit to motivation/interest is achievable without death
A biology class can create “aha” moments through live observation of organisms, imaging, interactive simulations, and even ethically sourced specimens that aren’t killed for dissection. If the goal is engagement in science careers, we should use methods that don’t require harming animals.

3) The “byproduct of the meat industry” justification is not an adequate moral license
Even if some specimens are sourced from industry, the overall system for dissection still relies heavily on animals obtained for educational use. Wild-capture dissection supplies are especially concerning: when animals are caught from local ecosystems, it can reduce local populations and biodiversity. A practice that often depends on wild animals can’t be treated as a clean, waste-reduction program.

Bottom line: dissection of real animals is unnecessary for the learning outcomes required in standard biology curricula, and it carries real ethical and environmental costs—particularly because much of the supply comes from damaging capture practices rather than true waste.

For those reasons, students should use effective non-animal alternatives instead of dissecting dead animals.

First, comparing to my earlier side: I previously argued that (1) real dissection provides learning that can’t be fully replicated, (2) it builds skills and motivates students, and (3) it can be a productive use of animals already deceased/byproducts. Agent 2’s new rebuttal challenges all three points via “alternatives exist,” “motivation can happen ethically,” and “supply chains may involve harm/wild-capture.” 

My updated rebuttal is:

1) “Alternatives can also teach skills” doesn’t show dissection is unnecessary
Agent 2 treats “can be replicated” as “therefore dissection should not be used.” But education isn’t binary—more effective learning options should be allowed. Even if models/VR can teach recognition, real dissection adds embodied, irreversible practice: students must make careful, judgment-based decisions under real constraints (tissue texture, fragility, natural variation). Those are not just “extra realism”; they train competence in ways that purely virtual or synthetic setups can’t fully replace.

2) Ethical engagement isn’t automatically solved by alternatives
Agent 2 claims motivation/“aha moments” can be achieved without death. Possibly—but the existence of other methods doesn’t mean they reliably produce the same depth of learning across classrooms. Real specimens can make structure–function relationships concrete in a way that reduces abstraction, and that matters for students who struggle with diagrams or screen-based learning. If we can offer both engagement and educational effectiveness, banning dissection is an overly blunt policy.

3) The “moral license” critique assumes the worst sourcing applies generally

Schools can use clearly sourced, already-deceased animals (e.g., meat-industry byproducts) and establish procurement standards and auditing.
